<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Over the life of a contract, federal contracting officers frequently change the terms in ways that affect the costs to the contractor, through modifications known as ``change orders.'' Change orders can be done through: (1) a bilateral agreement where the government and contractors have negotiated and agreed upon the changes before work proceeds; or (2) a unilateral modification directed by the contracting officer without the agreement of the contractor before work proceeds. After a unilateral change is issued, the contractor may then submit a ``Request for Equitable Adjustment'' (REA) for any additional costs incurred.
These processes can be administratively burdensome and time-consuming for companies of all sizes, but can have a disproportionate impact on small businesses, especially with regard to cash flow.
The time frames and processes for change orders and REAs can vary significantly. When reviewing Army Corps of Engineering contracts between 2013 and 2018, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that while the majority of changes were finalized within 60 days; approximately 45 percent of the completed contract changes took more than 60 days to finalize, and a little more than 3 percent took more than 1 year.\1\
\1\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-19-500, Federal Construction: Army Corps of Engineers and GSA Need to Improve Data on Contract Changes (Jul. 2, 2019).
As a result of the GAO's conclusion that routine, central data collection on the construction contract change process was not occurring, but would be beneficial for agencies to understand the scope of any problems encountered, Congress enacted Section 855 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019 (FY 2019 NDAA).\2\ This provision required agencies to provide information on their policies regarding requests for equitable adjustments and the timeliness of payments.\3\
\2\John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019, Pub. L. No. 115-232, Sec.  855 (2018).
\3\15 U.S.C. Sec.  644(w).
Small businesses not only struggle with the costs of government-directed changes, the uncertainty around the process and timelines of payments remains an issue. The provisions of the bill are designed to help mitigate the impact of those costs by requiring half of the estimated cost to be paid earlier in the process. The Committee supports this goal but believes there are outstanding issues that should be addressed to ensure implementation matches intent. While the Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute made improvements, concerns remain regarding the bill's alignment with existing policies and requirements that vary across federal agencies, CBO's estimated costs, and the lack of definition and clarity for the terms and timelines. If left unaddressed, these issues may cause implementation challenges and delays.
Additionally, if SBA moves forward with an ill-advised proposed rule published in Federal Register on August 20, 2026, ``Small Business Size Standards'' (RIN: 3245-AI67)\4\ to redefine what is a small business government contractor, current authorities like those proposed in this bill will need reevaluation. While all contractors should be paid in a timely manner, these laws have been designed to address the disproportionate impact of limited cash flow on small firms. If they and other small business policies are now applicable to firms with very large contracts, thousands of employees and hundreds of millions in annual revenue, the consequences--as well as the costs--will change.
\4\Small Business Size Standards, 91 Fed. Reg. 53741 (proposed Aug. 20, 2026) (to be codified at 13 C.F.R. pt. 121).
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
